newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore economy will grow despite Malaysia - MP.
newsitem.headline: Singapore economy will grow despite Malaysia - MP.

text.p: Singapore will not suffer a drop in foreign investment or economic growth because of competition from Malaysia, Singapore members of parliament said on Tuesday.

"As Malaysia improves economically, it is flexing its muscles and aims to overwhelm Singapore in diverting investments and trade," Chng Hee Kok of the ruling People's Action Party (PAP) told parliament.
But he said the volume of foreign direct investment into East Asia, estimated at around US$350 billion in 1995, was too vast for any country to dominate except China.
Nevertheless, ruling party members expressed worries over increasing competition with Malaysia.
A row broke out between the two countries earlier this year after former Singapore prime minister Lee Kuan Yew called the south Malaysian state of Johor notorious for crime.

Two apologies and the withdrawal of an affidavit in which Lee made the remark ended the row at government level, although relations remain strained. Newspapers in the two countries have continued sniping at each other, however.
The Singapore parliament, which began a new session on Monday, has expressed concern over the dispute and called for more awareness of increasing economic competition.
Chng said Malaysian multi-million dollar mega-projects such as the multi-media super corridor, a new seaport and a new Kuala Lumpur airport were aimed directly at Singapore.
"Their belief is that success in these projects will see lower investments in technology businesses into Singapore and decreasing the business done by our ports, Chng said.
"The days of 'beggar thy neighbour' policy is long gone and our neighbour must come to realise that economic competition is not a zero-sum game where there is a vanquished and a victor," he said.
Chng said newspaper reports of Singaporeans being delayed in Johor, unscheduled checks on investors and calls to boycott Singapore ports was not the way to encourage trade.
Inderjit Singh of the PAP also warned of competition.
"From the reactions of the Malaysian leaders recently, I hope Singaporeans realise that our close neighbour is all out to beat us as we compete," he said.
He said the large pool of talented professionals from Malaysia who work in Singapore's high-tech industries could be a problem.
"We must not underestimate the latent nationalist feeling that may exist among these professionals," Singh said.
He said if conditions became favourable in Malaysia, Singapore could encounter a reverse brain drain.
